findings.finding: Across 1,063 lead-generation quiz funnels on one platform, an average of 23.84% of visitors engage the quiz and 7.85% become leads (quizzes that are the page itself, with a lead form).
findings.quote: Across all landing page and embed formats, sampled from 1,063 live campaigns, lead generation quiz funnels capture a lead from 7.85% of visitors and engage 23.84%.
findings.context: ConvertFlow September 2026 benchmark: 1,063 live lead-generation quiz funnel campaigns sampled from its funnel database, means, denominator = visitors (not starters).
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. Vendor data from one platform, means only (no variance or significance), traffic is mostly sent to the quiz on purpose, and the page labels engagement "conversion rate". Not a cold reader finishing an article.
findings.implication: Treat about 1 in 4 visitors touching a quiz as the ceiling for a quiz that IS the page; an article reader who came for a fee or price will start less often, so track the click into the quiz as its own number.

findings.finding: Putting the quiz inside an existing page (embed) did not beat a dedicated quiz landing page: lead capture 10.45% embed vs 11.28% landing page, engagement 25.01% vs 26.72%.
findings.quote: Embedded lead generation quizzes capture a lead from 10.45% of visitors on average.
findings.context: Same ConvertFlow benchmark (n=1,063 campaigns). Same page also prints: landing-page quizzes capture a lead from 11.28% of visitors, convert (engage) 26.72%; embedded quizzes convert (engage) 25.01%.
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. Not an A/B test: different campaigns and host pages; gap is small and no significance is given; vendor, one platform.
findings.implication: An inline quiz module will not beat a button to a dedicated quiz page just by being inline; the lift must come from what the first step shows, so test it rather than assume it.

findings.finding: Quiz starters finish about 2 in 3 and give their contact about 4 in 10 (denominator = people who already started), so the hard step is the click to start, not completion.
findings.quote: Across the Interact portfolio, our long-term overall benchmarks are: Start-to-lead conversion rate: 40.1%.
findings.context: Interact 2026 report on its portfolio of lead-generation quizzes; the page states "Both start-to-finish and start-to-lead rates use quiz starts as the denominator." Service-provider quizzes: 42.2% start-to-lead, 47.3% start-to-finish. Start-to-finish 65% is stated on the same page.
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. Vendor reporting its own portfolio, no sample size printed, denominator is self-selected starters so it says nothing about how many visitors start.
findings.implication: Once someone taps the first photo she will probably continue, so put the effort into making the first tap visible and tempting on the guide page.

findings.finding: A supplement brand case study reports 65.4% of visitors took a quiz placed on the homepage, 44% of those who started completed it.
findings.number: 65.4% of visitors took the quiz; 44% completion of starters
findings.source_name: Octane AI via casestudies.com (vendor case study)
findings.quote: The quiz drove a 16× increase in email opt‑ins, saw 65.4% of visitors take the homepage quiz, achieved a 44% completion rate from those who start, and produced a 15.1% conversion rate from the quiz results page to purchase-delivering clear lift in engagement and conversions for Bariatric Fusion.
findings.context: One supplements brand (Bariatric Fusion, nutritional supplements for patients after weight-loss surgery) using Octane AI Shop Quiz on its homepage; also reports 16x email opt-ins and 15.1% quiz-results-page-to-purchase.
findings.caveat: WEAK. Single vendor-selected success story, "take the quiz" is not defined, e-commerce supplements, the quiz is the homepage rather than a side CTA on an informational page.
findings.implication: It shows an on-page quiz can reach most visitors when it is the first thing on the page; it is an argument to test an inline first question, not proof it works on an article page.

findings.finding: A multi-step "tool-like" form on a B2C lead-generation site raised conversion from 11% to 46%; the author also reports 0.96% to 8.1% on his own consulting form.
findings.quote: When we started using a multi-step 'tool-like' form on a B2C financial lead gen site we used to run our conversion rate increased from 11% to 46% .
findings.context: Venture Harbour (Marcus Taylor), same questions moved from one-step to multi-step; same page: consulting form 0.96% to 8.1% (a 743% increase in leads), Vendio +59% leads.
findings.caveat: WEAK-MEDIUM. Before/after on the author's own sites, not randomized A/B tests; the author's company sells the multi-step form tool (Leadformly) named on the page; sample sizes not printed.
findings.implication: Asking one small question at a time, tool-style, has the largest reported lifts of any form format, so the Dream Board's first photo tap should be built as that first small step.

findings.finding: In a controlled test the multi-step page beat the old page by 52.9% and the single-step page by 40.3%, so multi-step won only modestly over single-step.
findings.number: +52.9% multi-step vs +40.3% single-step (vs control), ~1,100 visits per variation
findings.quote: Well, the new streamlined page leveraging the multiple steps improved the conversions over the control by 52.9%.
findings.context: Conversion Fanatics, July 2015: three variations (old control, streamlined multi-step, streamlined single-step), "just over 1100 visits per variation", 151 extra leads for multi-step and 91 extra for single-step vs control; the agency notes that past tests often show multi-step reducing conversions.
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. One client, agency write-up, both variants also streamlined the page so the gain over control mixes cleaner design with step count; multi vs single difference not tested for significance.
findings.implication: Do not expect multi-step alone to carry the result; the cleaner, simpler page mattered about as much, so keep the guide page CTA block short and visual.

findings.finding: Across 10 split tests on its own landing pages, a button that opens a popup form (2-step) converted 44% and the form placed on the page (1-step) converted 45%, i.e. no gain from the extra click.
findings.quote: One-step opt-in forms had an average conversion rate of 45% (vs. 44%) and a higher weighted average across all 10 landing page split tests.
findings.context: Leadpages marketing team: 10 landing-page split tests on lead-magnet pages; popup form won 4 tests, on-page form won 6, weighted average also favored on-page by "a hair".
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. Vendor's own pages, email opt-in for a lead magnet (not a quiz), traffic volumes varied and margins were narrow.
findings.implication: A button that merely opens the quiz adds no lift by itself; the interactive step has to be worth tapping (a real photo choice) rather than just postponing a form.

findings.finding: A large popup dataset shows a first micro-commitment click (yes/no or preference) before asking for contact details converts at 5.64% vs 3.07% for single-step, an 84% lift.
findings.quote: In a Wisepops study of 1.8 million visitor sessions, micro-commitment and multi-step formats drove up to 8-9× more interactions and doubled signups vs. standard single-step popups - with no increase in bounce Multi-step popups average a 5.64% conversion rate vs. 3.07% for single-step - an 84% increase
findings.context: Wisepops, published March 2026: 1.8 million visitor sessions across its customers; "up to 8-9x more interactions" and doubled signups for micro-commitment and multi-step formats; the page also lists survey/preference-selector popup templates.
findings.caveat: WEAK-MEDIUM. Vendor reporting its own customers, method and controls not described, popups (not static pages), "up to" figures are best cases.
findings.implication: The pattern with the biggest vendor-measured upside is a tiny first choice (for example "which of these looks like your wedding?") before any commitment, which is exactly the Dream Board's first tap.

findings.finding: Typeform reports that forms featuring images or video complete 120.6% more often than forms without them (observational, across its users).
findings.source_name: Typeform via MarTech Series press release
findings.quote: Incorporate visuals: Forms that feature images or video see a 120.6% increase in completion rates over forms that don't.
findings.context: Typeform "Data On Data" report (2023 data, aggregated trends over 10 years); the same release gives an overall average completion rate of 47.3% vs an industry average of 21.5%.
findings.caveat: WEAK. Vendor press release (typeform.com itself could not be read), observational comparison of forms, not an A/B test, "images" is not specific to image-choice questions, selection effects likely.
findings.implication: Directional support for leading with real wedding photos, not text, in the first step; do not quote 120.6% as an expected lift.

findings.finding: A field experiment on loyalty cards found 34% redeemed a card that came with 2 stamps already filled vs 19% of customers with an empty card needing the same number of purchases.
findings.source_name: Game Developer (secondhand summary of Nunes & Dreze 2006)
findings.quote: They found that 34 percent of people who received a ten-stamp card with two freebies ended up coming back enough to redeem the cards, compared to 19 percent of customers who started with an unstamped card requiring only eight stamps.
findings.context: Car-wash loyalty-card experiment by Nunes and Dreze (Journal of Consumer Research, 2006): both groups needed eight purchases; one card had ten slots with two free stamps. Page also says the stamped group returned faster.
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. Secondhand magazine summary; the original paper was not opened; offline loyalty card, not a web page; sample size not printed on this page.
findings.implication: Show progress as already started ("Step 1 of 3", one example photo pre-picked) instead of an empty board, because artificial head starts raised completion in the best-known test.

findings.finding: Original foot-in-the-door experiment: housewives who first did a small soap survey agreed to a large home-inventory request about 53% of the time vs about 22% when asked cold.
findings.source_name: Atticus Li blog (secondhand account of Freedman & Fraser 1966)
findings.quote: The compliance rate for women who'd done the small survey first: about 53%.
findings.context: Freedman and Fraser 1966, Experiment 1 (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 4, 195-202); the same page gives the cold-call control as about 22%. The PubMed abstract of the 2020 direct replication (PMID 31475878) says "the effect size obtained by Freedman and Fraser in their studies has never been obtained again" and the effect vanished in its 2013 groups.
findings.caveat: WEAK. Secondhand blog; the 1966 paper PDF could not be read; original effect is known to be much larger than later replications and meta-analyses.
findings.implication: The idea that a small first ask raises the next ask is real but the famous size is not reliable, so test the first-photo-tap against a plain button instead of assuming a doubling.

findings.finding: Meta-analytic calibration: 120 foot-in-the-door experiment groups from 1966-1981 gave a small effect, and nearly half the studies showed no effect or the opposite.
findings.number: 120 groups; probit effect about 0.32; about half no/negative effect
findings.source_name: Atticus Li blog (secondhand account of Beaman et al. 1983 meta-analysis)
findings.quote: Beaman et al. examined 120 experimental groups from 1966-1981 and found a probit effect size of about 0.32 - small but statistically significant. They also noted that nearly half the studies showed no effect or effects in the opposite direction.
findings.context: The page summarises Beaman, Cole, Preston, Klentz and Steblay (1983), "Fifteen Years of Foot-in-the-Door Research: A Meta-Analysis" (Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin).
findings.caveat: WEAK-MEDIUM. Secondhand blog summary, the 1983 paper was not opened; the blog also attributes r about 0.17 to Burger 1999 but Burger 1999 is a review and I could not confirm that figure, so it is not used.
findings.implication: Commitment-and-consistency is a probabilistic edge, not a mechanism to build the page around; keep the plain button as the control in any test.

findings.finding: Changing a button from second person ("Get your 30-day trial") to first person ("Get my free 30-day trial") raised click-through 90% on an Unbounce PPC landing page.
findings.quote: In this case, we saw a 90% increase in click through rate when we tested Get my free 30-day trial against Get your 30-day trial
findings.context: Aagaard and Oli Gardner on an Unbounce PPC landing page; the page is dated October 16th, 2013 and says he later saw lifts from "My" over "Your" on a number of other sites without printing their numbers.
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. One test, 2013, measured on click-through (not signups); the two buttons also differ by the word "free" (only the "my" button has it), so the 90% mixes pronoun and "free"; sample size not printed.
findings.implication: Write the button in first person and name what she gets ("Show me my Dream Board, free"), and A/B it against the plain version since the best-known figure is a single confounded test.

findings.finding: On a payment page, the button with "Your" converted 24.95% worse than the control that used "My".
findings.quote: When I tested live on the website, it turned out that the treatment with "Your" performed significantly worse than the control copy that made use of "My" - 24.95% worse to be more precise
findings.context: Aagaard's test on the payment page (last funnel step) of a client; he writes his hypothesis was that "Your" would win and that the experience comes from "almost 400 split tests".
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. One client, one test, sample size not printed; the page's own heading says 26.55% while the body says 24.95%, so the exact figure is unsettled.
findings.implication: First-person wording has the best published support where the click leads to something that becomes hers (her board, her dress list).

findings.finding: Changing one word in a call to action ("Order" to "Get", which names what you receive) lifted conversions 38.26% on an office-rental portal.
findings.quote: Here's an example from a case study where changing one word in the call-to-action on a B2B site generated a 38.26% lift in conversions.
findings.context: Case study of a B2B portal listing offices for rent where the CTA asks for lease information by email; the page explains "Order" stresses what you must do while "Get" stresses what you receive.
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. Single agency case study, B2B, sample size not printed, the before/after labels are inferred from the explanation sentence.
findings.implication: Name the thing she receives ("Get my matching dresses") rather than the chore ("Start quiz", "Submit").

findings.finding: Making a generic call to action ("Get membership") specific to the visitor's situation by adding "Find gym" lifted conversions 68% on a gym chain PPC page.
findings.quote: Here's another case study that shows how adding relevance to a call-to-action can have a dramatic effect on conversions - in this case a 68% lift.
findings.context: Anonymous major gym chain in Scandinavia; PPC landing page whose goal is a click to the checkout flow whose first step is choosing a gym.
findings.caveat: MEDIUM. Single case study, anonymous client, sample size not printed.
findings.implication: A button that names the concrete first action matched to why she came ("Pick my courthouse-wedding look") should beat a generic "Get started".

findings.finding: HubSpot reports calls to action personalised to the visitor convert 202% better than basic ones, from 330,000+ CTAs over six months.
findings.quote: After analyzing and comparing more than 330,000 CTAs over a six-month timeframe, we discovered that personalized CTAs convert 202% better than basic CTAs.
findings.context: HubSpot analysis of its own CTA tool; the page describes personalising by location, device, referral source or language.
findings.caveat: MEDIUM-WEAK. Vendor figure, method and baseline not described, "personalized" means targeted by visitor attributes, not a copy change, and it is relative lift.
findings.implication: Use a different CTA on each guide page (courthouse fees, small-venue prices, secondhand dresses) that matches that page's topic, rather than one generic block everywhere.

findings.finding: On over 40,000 HubSpot-customer landing pages, buttons left as the default "Submit" tended to convert worse than buttons with other wording.
findings.number: n=40,000+ landing pages (no lift printed); n=400 preference test
findings.quote: I found that landing pages with submit buttons actually labeled "submit" tended to have lower conversion rates than those that used other wording.
findings.context: Zarrella compared pages that kept the default "Submit" to pages that changed it; a separate context-free test with "over 400 people" found "click here" and "go" top, which he says feel less committal.
findings.caveat: WEAK. Sample size is the only number: no lift is printed, it is observational (pages that changed the label may differ otherwise), the 400-person test had no real stakes, and the post is an old one (the page shows "Updated: 06/06/25"), so the age of the data is unclear.
findings.implication: Never ship a generic "Submit" or "Start"; use a specific verb phrase for the outcome she gets.

findings.finding: Academic evidence for the word "free": in a chocolate choice experiment, when the cheaper Hershey's Kiss went from 1 cent to free (and the Lindt truffle fell from 15 to 14 cents), its share of choices among buyers rose from 27% to 69%.
findings.quote: 27% in the 1&15 condition to 69% in the 0&14 condi-
findings.context: Experiment 2, real purchases of chocolate in a field setting; the full sentence reads "...the share of Hershey's increases from 27% in the 1&15 condition to 69% in the 0&14 condition and to 64% in the 0&10 condition" after removing the participants coded as choosing nothing. The sentence is split by a column break and a hyphenated line end in the PDF.
findings.caveat: WEAK for web copy. A price effect on physical goods, not a test of the word "free" in a button; its Experiment 6 separately forces deliberate evaluation to probe the mechanism; the fragment quoted ends at a hyphenated line break because the PDF is two-column.
findings.implication: A free app is genuinely at zero price, so "free" is worth stating once next to the button (not as a badge on every line), but no web CTA test isolating the word was found.

no_evidence: QUIZ: first question shown inline on the page vs a "start" button: Octane AI help (help.octaneai.com, updated March 2026) says a quiz can get a higher first-page click-through by jumping straight into the first question, but prints no number; no A/B test with a lift was found.

QUIZ: Roobrik (a consumer-planning self-assessment, senior living) reports a landing-page test that raised starts by 15%, but its page never says which variation won (one variant "incorporated" the first question), so no inline-question conclusion can be drawn.

QUIZ: image-choice (tap photos) vs text-choice questions: no controlled test found beyond the Typeform images/video aggregate; the academic image-answer papers found concern open-ended survey questions, not quiz choices.
QUIZ: GoodUI pattern #9 "Multiple Steps" lists 14 tests (3 on signup, 4 on home and landing) but the lift numbers are behind a paid membership, so nothing could be quoted.

QUIZ: Octane AI "quiz start rate industry average 45%" (octaneai.com) could not be read without JavaScript and has no stated method; Outgrow (start rate 40-60%, completion 65-85% for 3-7 questions) and Visual Quiz Builder (start rate 20-40%) print ranges with no sample or method, so they are excluded.
QUIZ: Heyflow, Perspective, Jotform, Formstack: no published benchmark with method found (Heyflow shows individual case studies of 13-21%; Formstack's 13.85% vs 4.53% only appears secondhand).
QUIZ: NN/g and Baymard: no number on quiz funnels or on a first-step commitment found; NN/g only states without figures that progress indicators motivate users to continue.
QUIZ: primary text of Freedman & Fraser 1966 and Nunes & Dreze 2006 could not be read (PDFs unreachable); numbers are secondhand.

WORDING: wedding or consumer-planning CTA copy tests ("Start planning", "Get started", "Build my board"): none found published with numbers (Greenvelope/Mixpanel tested an award badge, not copy, and prints no result).
WORDING: a controlled test isolating the word "free" in a button: none found; the only "free" number comes in the Aagaard 90% test where "free" is confounded with "my", plus a lab price study.

WORDING: button size or contrast: no primary source with sample sizes was found within the time box (Demio +57.79% and Kommunicate +25.5% appear only in a HubSpot roundup of other firms' tests, so they are not used).

WORDING: the essay-site example on the Unbounce CTA page ("Read Full Essay Now" beating "Get Instant Access Now" on pages that preview an essay, 120,000+ pages) is the closest analogue to a preview-then-click guide page, but the page prints no number for it.
notes: Evidence strength is tagged at the start of each caveat (STRONG/MEDIUM/WEAK); nothing here is STRONG because there is no independent, randomized, large-sample quiz-vs-button test on an informational page. Best-supported items: Unbounce/Aagaard first-person and specific-outcome button copy tests (primary page, single tests), ConvertFlow n=1,063 quiz benchmark, Leadpages 10-test counter-evidence that a click-to-open step alone does not help. Aagaard's 90% (my vs your) is confounded with the word "free" and the same page contradicts itself on the payment-page figure (26.55% heading vs 24.95% body). The Duke PDF quote is a line fragment because the verifier reads two-column PDFs with pdftotext -layout. No git, GitHub or other files were touched; raw pages are in .cache/raw/conv/r2/.
